original_value: Development of convolutional neural network (CNN) optimized for object detection, led to significant developments in ship detection. Although training data critically affect the performance of the CNN-based training model, previous studies focused mostly on enhancing the architecture of the training model. This study developed a sophisticated and automatic methodology to generate verified and robust training data by employing synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images and automatic identification system (AIS) data. The extraction of training data initiated from interpolating the discretely received AIS positions to the exact position of the ship at the time of image acquisition. The interpolation was conducted by applying a Kalman filter, followed by compensating the Doppler frequency shift. The bounding box for the ship was constructed tightly considering the installation of the AIS equipment and the exact size of the ship. From 18 Sentinel-1 SAR images using a completely automated procedure, 7489 training data were obtained, compared with a different set of training data from visual interpretation. The ship detection model trained using the automatic training data obtained 0.7713 of overall detection performance from 3 Sentinel-1 SAR images, which exceeded that of manual training data, evading the artificial structures of harbors and azimuth ambiguity ghost signals from detection.

result.paraphrase: CNN-based object detection has driven major advances in ship detection. Since training data have a critical impact on CNN training model performance, earlier studies mostly concentrated on improving the model architecture. This study instead created a sophisticated automated method for producing verified, robust training data using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images and automatic identification system (AIS) data. Training data extraction began by interpolating the discretely received AIS positions to the ship’s exact location at the time of image acquisition. A Kalman filter was used for the interpolation, followed by Doppler frequency-shift compensation. The ship bounding box was then drawn tightly, taking into account the AIS equipment installation and the ship’s exact size. Using a fully automated procedure on 18 Sentinel-1 SAR images, 7489 training samples were obtained, and these were compared with a separate set of training data derived from visual interpretation. The ship detection model trained with the automated data achieved an overall detection performance of 0.7713 on 3 Sentinel-1 SAR images, outperforming manual training data and avoiding harbor artificial structures and azimuth ambiguity ghost signals in detection.
